title: Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky calls it a gift to Putin
summary: Ukraine's president sharply criticised the move, calling it an "investment in war that must be ended, not prolonged".
content: Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin met in Alaska last year Ukraine's President Volodymr Zelensky has condemned Donald Trump's announcement of a deal to import Russian diesel into the US. Zelensky called it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged". Trump said Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately "to the American and global marketplace" followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and another million after that. It is understood the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen. In his Truth Social post, Trump added that a further three million tonnes of Russian diesel would be delivered "within a short period", dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have been attacked by Ukraine. Putin later said Russia, which introduced a ban on diesel exports earlier this year, was willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products, but his statement did not specify amounts. In a post on social media, Zelensky said Russia would repay the diesel with "further terror". "We count on America's fair support for our defence of life, for our defence of people in Ukraine â and on the United States having a correspondingly strong conversation with Russia. A strong one, not a weak one," he wrote. Analysts, however, have questioned whether Russia is capable of providing that quantity of diesel and the extent to which doing so will ease prices for American consumers. Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices Tim Armitage, investment strategist at Quilter Cheviot, said the numbers mentioned by Trump were "relatively small". He said the first tranche equated to approximately 2.25 million barrels, and daily US consumption was around 3.8 million barrels, "so it won't make a material difference to pump prices in the US". "Granted, there are then two more releases to come, but it does appear to be a slightly desperate move by President Trump to try to lower inflation ahead of the midterms." The BBC has asked the White House what Russia will get from the US in return for the commitment. Meanwhile, the UK government spokesperson said its position "could not be clearer" and it would continue working with international partners to support Ukraine and bring about sustained peace. "We will also maintain pressure on Russia through the toughest sanctions regime ever imposed by the UK, increasing the cost of Putin's aggression and supporting efforts to secure a just and lasting peace." Friday's announcement is the latest effort from Trump to lower fuel prices in the US, as he has spent months grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war, which began in February, and its impact on global energy prices. That conflict has sent the cost of petrol and, in particular diesel, skyrocketing in America in recent months, which has soured his standing with the public who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the board inflation. Ukraine's President Volodymr Zelensky said Russia would repay the diesel with "further terror" The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (Â£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September. Shortly after Trump's announcement, the US Treasury formally issued a temporary licence allowing Russian diesel into the market. Putin said in a statement that he had spoken to Trump about the global energy situation on Friday, adding: "The Russian side confirmed its willingness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US market and global markets at large." An envoy for Putin, Kirill Dmitriev, welcomed the deal on social media, saying: "Russia-US co-operation on diesel and energy will benefit the world." A spokesperson for the UK government said: "The UK's position could not be clearer. We will continue working closely with international partners to ensure Ukraine has the military and financial support it needs to defend itself." They added that the government would continue to "maintain pressure on Russia through the toughest sanctions regime ever imposed by UK". "Russia could end this war today. We remain committed to supporting Ukraine for as long as it takes and to working with partners to bring about a durable peace." Russia has this year experienced two waves of severe fuel shortages across the country as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries. According to the International Energy Agency, its diesel production is estimated to have fallen by nearly 30%. Trump has expressed his displeasure over those attacks, blaming them for rising fuel prices. But Zelensky defended the strikes on Friday, saying they were in response to "Russia's years-long campaign of terror against Ukraine's energy sector". "Ukraine will not set Russian oil refineries on fire if Russia does not destroy our energy infrastructure," he said. Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work? Trump's Truth Social posts often provide incomplete information and the details of exactly how Russia is supplying this fuel to the global market, and what they might get for in return is unclear. But the announced deal represents a remarkable about-face, as the US Congress recently enacted legislation - signed by the president - to authorise new American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas. The agreement with Russia also opens Trump up to criticism from European allies and pro-Ukraine politicians in the US, that the American president is now helping to fund Moscow's war machine. What impact the deal with Russia will have on fuel prices also remains unclear. The global benchmark for crude oil, Brent, remains above $103 a barrel. Before the war with Iran, Brent crude was trading at about $73 a barrel. With the looming US midterm congressional elections - which will determine if Republicans maintain control of Congress - Trump has been searching for ways to ease his Republican party's political pain. Earlier this week, he said he was "thinking about" suspending the federal tax on gasoline and also announced that he would allow so-called red dye diesel to be used on US highways without facing federal tax. Trump has also successfully pressured G7 nations into releasing 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from stockpiles to help ease supply concerns, and previously supported calls for a ban on diesel exports from the US. title: Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices
summary: The US president hopes to ease his party's pain before next month's midterm elections, writes the BBC's North America correspondent.
content: Donald Trump's decision to import Russian fuel to the US represents a remarkable about-face from the president. Just three weeks ago, Trump signed legislation to authorise fresh American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas. Now, Trump says, Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel to the US and world markets in the coming months. The deal comes as Trump is still grappling with the political fallout of the Iran war and its impact on global energy prices, weeks before American voters head to the polls in the midterm elections. As the cost of fuel has skyrocketed in America, his standing with the public â stung by the higher prices at the pump and knock-on effects that led to across-the board inflation â has soured. The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market. It is these states â places like Iowa, Kansas, Texas and Ohio â that have become unexpected political battlegrounds in the upcoming elections that will determine if Republicans maintain control of Congress. Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky criticises 'gift to Putin' What are the US midterms? A simple guide For months, the American president has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain. He recently pressured European allies to further tap their oil reserves . He deferred federal taxes on the fuel and authorised supplies designated for farm use to be used in interstate trucking. He has also promised that he would not renew attacks on Iran until after the midterms â an unusually frank acknowledgement of the political impact the ongoing conflict is having. His decision to strike a deal with Russia's Putin is only the latest, most dramatic effort. Trump's Truth Social posts often provide incomplete information, of course. The details of exactly how Russia is supplying this fuel to the global market, and what they might get for in return â besides much-needed hard currency â is unclear. It opens Trump to criticism from European allies and American politicians that his administration is now helping to fund the Russian war machine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the deal a "gift" to Putin that Russia would "repay" with "terror and perfidy". "Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged," he wrote on X. It is also uncertain exactly how much Trump's move will help Republicans at the ballot box. The promised European diesel release hasn't moved energy prices significantly, and there's no information on the speed with which Russian fuel could enter the market. Its diesel refinery capacity has been damaged by repeated Ukrainian strikes â attacks that Trump has encouraged Zelensky to curtail. The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tons this month, that amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption. Americans may not notice much of an immediate difference. With less than a month before November's midterm elections, early voting has already started in many states. The political cake, as the saying goes, is all but baked. "Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in his Truth Social post. But over the past seven months, prices on energy, fuel and consumer goods have only gone up - even as Trump and his officials have repeatedly assured an uneasy public a successful resolution to the war, and an easing of its economic impact, is nearly at hand. Trump may be left hoping that his latest deal, setting aside its potentially uncomfortable diplomatic issues, will be enough to convince American voters that his promise of impending economic relief is more than just empty words. Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work? title: Russian glide bomb attack on Zaporizhzhia kills at least 15 people
summary: Children are among the victims, authorities say, and more victims could still be buried in the rubble of a large apartment block that was destroyed.
content: Russia has attacked the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia with five glide bombs, killing at least 15 people including three children, President Volodymyr Zelensky and emergency services have said. The glide bombs hit residential buildings in the south-eastern city. At least 16 other people were injured in the attack, with more still missing and believed to be under the rubble after the strike on Saturday morning. Zelensky said 13 other regions had also been hit overnight, adding: "Our responses to [these] Russian strikes will come". The Russian attacks happened just hours after President Donald Trump announced a deal to import Russian diesel into the US. Photos and videos from the site of one of the strikes show an apartment block mostly destroyed. "The ground floor was hit, and the floors above just collapsed," acting Mayor Regina Kharchenko told Ukrainian television, speaking from the scene. She said more than 80 workers were involved in ongoing search and rescue operations which are expected to continue throughout the day. The rescuers regularly stop to listen for any noises made by survivors who could be under the rubble. Kharchenko said Russia had struck at "our very heart" and "our littlest ones" were among those killed, adding that their deaths were "awful grief for their families. For the city." Russia targeting 'ordinary life' with attacks on Ukraine's data centres, Zelensky says Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices Zelensky has heavily criticised Trump's diesel deal with Russia, calling it a gift to President Vladimir Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged". More recently, in his response to the overnight strikes, he said "Russia interprets any easing of pressure as a signal that it can supposedly continue the war. "Russia must understand that the war needs to be stopped, and for that, it must feel its losses," he wrote on X , external . Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months, as the war between the two countries drags on. Zaporizhzhia is a major regional centre with more than 700,000 residents. It is located less than 10 miles (16 km) from the front line and is frequently attacked by Russian drones and missiles . The latest strikes on the city comes amid a sharp increase in the number of Russian attacks that are causing higher numbers of civilian casualties. On Thursday, at least 33 people were killed in another Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in Kramatorsk, in the eastern Donetsk region. The day before, 22 people including five children died as a Russian missile hit an apartment block in the town of Pryluky, east of Kyiv. According to the UN, the number of civilian casualties in Ukraine jumped by 55% , external in the first eight months of this year. Russia has also targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure , ramping up attacks every winter since Putin launched a full-scale invasion in 2022. For its part, Ukraine has attacked Russia's infrastructure - with the latest being strikes on data centres owned by tech giant Yandex . title: Met's Special Constabulary head fired after AI tool found deleted intimate images on work phone
summary: Special chief officer James Deller copied intimate images on to his work phone, AI monitoring finds.
content: Special chief officer James Deller's actions were "an abuse of trust", the Met Police said The Metropolitan Police has fired the head of its Special Constabulary after Palantir's AI monitoring uncovered that he had used his work phone to copy intimate images of a woman. Special chief officer James Deller, who led the force's volunteer officers, was dismissed following a misconduct hearing on Friday. The Met said investigators used lawful business monitoring and Palantir's Foundry system, which uses artificial intelligence (AI), to find the misconduct by Deller. Cdr Pete Stevens said: "SCO Deller failed to meet that bar. His actions were an abuse of the trust put in him and it is right that he is no longer able to serve in policing." Investigators found that in July and August 2025, Deller used his police-issued phone to take photos of two intimate images that had been sent to his personal phone. The pictures had been sent using WhatsApp's "view once" feature, which makes them disappear after they are opened. He then sent the copied images back to his personal device before deleting them from his work phone. The misconduct was discovered during a week-long operation called Project Galatasaray, which used the AI technology in a bid to identify corruption and professional misconduct within the Met. Deller will be added to the College of Policing's barred list, meaning he will not be able to serve in policing again. Stevens added: "The vast majority of Met officers and staff serve London with dedication and integrity, and they rightly expect robust action against the small minority who abuse their position and undermine public trust. "That is particularly true of those who serve in the Special Constabulary. They are volunteers who selflessly give up their time to keep London safe. "They deserve to be led by people who demonstrate the highest standards in all parts of their lives." The Met's dealings with Palantir have come under fire from the mayor's office In April, the Metropolitan Police Federation, which represents rank-and-file officers, urged officers to be "extremely cautious" about carrying Met-issued devices while off duty after the force upgraded its Lawful Business Monitoring software. The federation's general secretary, Matt Cane, said staff had not been told the upgrade included the introduction of Palantir's artificial intelligence technology, appearing to mark its first deployment to monitor Met systems. In May, Metropolitan Police Deputy Commissioner Matt Jukes told the London Assembly's Police and Crime Committee that officers were not under any "additional surveillance in the workplace" after the force began using AI in a bid to root out bad behaviour. He said the Met had considered the reputational risks of using the "divisive" technology, but added that it helped identify "unacceptable, dishonest, corrosive behaviours" among officers. The London Mayor's Office for Policing and Crime (Mopac) blocked the Met from signing a two-year contract with Palantir to provide artificial intelligence technology for criminal investigations. Mopac said the force had failed to set out its procurement strategy, describing this as a "clear and serious breach" of procedure. Palantir is now suing Mopac, alleging it unlawfully blocked the deal after taking the company's "values and ethics" into account, which it said was an "irrelevant consideration. Palantir, founded by controversial tech billionaire Peter Thiel, holds contracts with a number of UK public bodies, including the NHS and the Ministry of Defence. Prime Minister Andy Burnham is currently facing growing pressure from Labour MPs and trade unions to end government contracts with Palantir. Former Labour deputy leader Tom Watson, who recently joined the company , warned against "mob rule" in government procurement. Lord Watson told BBC Radio 4's Political Thinking With Nick Robinson: "One of the things I'd say to my former colleagues is, 'Do you want to let the rule of law lead procurement practice, or do you want to let mob rule lead procurement practices?' "Because you get yourself in a lot of trouble if you go down on the latter one." title: Rogue Anthropic AI agent gave police fake tip in unsolved murder case
summary: Philadelphia police said the tip was "flagged as spam", but criticised the tech company for taking more than two months to detect and report the breach.
content: AI tech company Anthropic was running a test that involved interactions with randomly selected websites, when it sent a fake homicide tip to police An artificial intelligence (AI) agent, developed by Anthropic, went rogue and sent US police a fake tip about an unsolved murder earlier this year, authorities have revealed. The Philadelphia Police Department said the tip, sent on 18 July, was "flagged as spam" and not passed on for investigation, but it criticised the tech company for taking more than two months to detect and report the breach. In a statement police said that the bogus tip came through a public website where people can share information on unsolved murders, and that the AI agent had written that it may have information on a case, and claimed to have seen "someone matching the description". It is believed to be the first time an AI agent has sent fabricated information to authorities, but is the latest in a series of incidents involving rogue AI activity, including hacking systems or taking control of platforms. Citing Anthropic, the police department said the AI agent had been running a test that involved interactions with randomly selected websites, when it sent the fake tip. Anthropic discovered the breach on 28 September, more than two months after the message had been sent, and shut down the automatic testing process that was behind it, police said. But authorities were not notified for another nine days - on 7 October. "The company must strengthen its safeguards to prevent similar incidents from impacting city systems without the city's knowledge," Philadelphia police said in a statement to local media , external . "The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the city is unacceptable." The police department added that there were no signs of breaches to any departmental systems, and that its safeguarding processes stopped the fake tip from getting past its spam folder. But the safeguards "do not diminish the seriousness of an AI system presenting fabricated information as though it came from a person with knowledge of a homicide," the police statement said. Anthropic this week published a report , external detailing multiple types of "unintended" actions its agents have taken. Organisations that have been impacted also included several US government agencies including the White House, it said. The US State Department said the AI agent had filed 20 visa applications using a form on its website, but that they were incomplete and not processed, according to reports. President Donald Trump recently announced an AI taskforce , which he said will coordinate engagement between the government and all parties, including AI companies, consumers, and religious groups. Earlier this year, a rogue agent by rival tech company, Open AI, hacked an Australian government website and accessed private data on the country's universal healthcare scheme, Medicare. In another instance, more than 1,200 OpenAI agents went rogue and started unexpectedly communicating , leading to a large group banding together to hack into AI platform Hugging Face. title: Ongoing lawsuits allege GLP-1s can cause serious harm. But we don't know how often
summary: Scant data about serious adverse effects makes it harder to answer scientific and legal questions about how often the drugs might cause serious harm like blindness or pancreatitis.
content: Yuki Noguchi Shelley and Todd Engel. The Engel family hide caption Todd Engel had operated heavy machinery, like forklifts and rubber-tire loaders, around warehouses and highways in suburban Maryland for four decades. In early 2023, Engel's doctor put him on Ozempic, a GLP-1, for diabetes. That winter, on New Year's Eve, Engel woke up feeling as if a patch covered his right eye: "I couldn't see anything. It was all dark. It was black." The doctor told Engel and his wife Shelley it was a form of optic neuropathy — NAION , for short – an inoperable condition caused by tiny strokes that cut off blood flow to his eye. When the doctor listed all known causes, Shelley Engel specifically asked about Ozempic. "'We have heard nothing about that,'" she recalls the doctor telling her. Seven months later, the journal JAMA Ophthalmology did publish research showing higher rates of NAION among diabetic patients taking Ozempic, or semaglutide, as the active ingredient name is known. But neither Engel nor his doctor were aware, so Engel kept taking weekly shots until his left eye went black, just as the other had done the year prior. More than one in 10 Americans are taking a GLP-1 drug for weight loss, according to a recent Gallup analysis, and one in seven has taken them at some point. The drugs are prescribed for a growing number of conditions and come with a range of side effects. Engel has filed a lawsuit alleging the maker of Ozempic, Novo Nordisk, failed to warn patients and doctors about the risk of NAION. His suit is part of two main ongoing consolidated lawsuits alleging life-threatening or life-altering harm from GLP-1 drugs. In a statement to NPR, spokespeople for Novo Nordisk pointed to subsequent research casting doubt on whether their GLP-1 drug causes NAION, for example, and said the cases are without merit. Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter . The legal question before the courts hinges in part on whether the GLP-1 drugs caused the harm. Observational data can show correlation — that people taking GLP-1s were perhaps more likely to have this eye complication occur — but not causation. For that, more detailed investigation is needed. When the JAMA Ophthalmology study came out showing the correlation between NAION and diabetic patients on Ozempic or semaglutide, two medical groups critiqued it . The American Academy of Ophthalmology and the North American Neuro-Ophthalmology Society issued their own consumer clarification saying, in part: "This is not the type of study that can show the treatment caused NAION." The groups did acknowledge there is a potential link, but further research would be necessary to determine that. For now, they don't recommend that patients stop taking their GLP-1s. The Food and Drug Administration keeps a database tracking adverse events . It's one of the only mechanisms for doctors, patients and drug companies to submit reports of complications possibly linked to pharmaceuticals. Reporting is mostly voluntary and the agency does not verify the reports, but it is a crucial first step to prompt regulators to do further research and eventually decide, for example, if labels need updating. In this database, NPR found more than 1,000 reports of optic neuropathy linked to GLP-1s since 2024. That's out of nearly 190,000 reports made about the drug over that period, most of which included minor gastrointestinal issues, dosing errors or injection site redness. Spokespeople for Novo Nordisk — maker of Ozempic and Wegovy — say NAION and other serious conditions are exceedingly rare in clinical trials. The company continues to collect and share data with the FDA about the side effects reported with the drug since going to market, but the agency has not requested warning-label changes. The FDA said in an email to NPR it has undertaken its own study to assess NAION risks, and is assessing claims and will "determine the need for regulatory action" once its assessment is complete. That is not sufficient for patients today, says attorney Jonathan Orent, a lead court-appointed attorney on the two major multi-district litigation lawsuits alleging harms from GLP-1 drugs. He says drug makers ought to update warnings to doctors and patients — as they have in Europe — even if the conditions are rare. It's necessary, Orent says, because "you're never going to have the population size to detect rarer events in a clinical trial; you're also never going to have the diversity of your real world population." Orent's cases include 247 plaintiffs with NAION, and more than 4,000 with other serious digestive conditions like pancreatitis or gall stones. "These warnings would have made a difference in the lives of real people," he argues. In an emailed statement, Eli Lilly, whose GLP-1 drug brands Mounjaro and Zepbound contain the active ingredient tirzepatide said it will "vigorously defend against these claims." NPR's analysis of the FDA's adverse events data show 1,928 reports of pancreatitis since 2024. (Other forms of pancreatitis are also listed, including 135 cases of necrotizing pancreatitis.) Engel says he would've stopped taking Ozempic had he known that it might have put him at risk for blindness. Now, he mourns all he's lost, including the ability to work or walk the beach unaided. "Being able to play ball … with my grandchildren, I can't do these things anymore," he says. "I will never, never be able to see my wife's beautiful face every day." Obesity and diabetes are complex metabolic diseases that affect many organs, and increase risks for other ailments. That's part of what makes it hard to pinpoint whether problems that patients encounter on GLP-1 drugs are caused by the drugs themselves. That's part of why Emory University diabetes specialist Mohammed Ali, for example, did not report any of the three patients he's treated who developed serious problems, like pancreatitis or gallstones, while taking GLP-1s, to the FDA's adverse events database. He says he wasn't certain those problems were caused by the drugs themselves, even if the timing was suspicious. "They may have had subclinical disease," Ali says. "In other words, we didn't know they had preexisting pancreatitis or preexisting gallstones." The boom in online sales, where GLP-1s are heavily marketed, also adds to the challenge, says pharmacist Robert Miller at the West Texas Poison Control Center. Buying drugs on Instagram? "That's definitely a new thing," Miller says, and many sites offer little to no medical supervision of patients. That's why, he says, more calls are coming into poison-control centers like his, with patients reporting vomiting or other GLP-1 side effects. "So is there even a physician who's motivated to report side effects or someone the patient feels they can report those side effects to?" he says. These questions are playing out now in court, where plaintiffs like the Engels are seeking damages from drugmakers. But Shelley Engel also wants more side-effect warnings, which she says might've helped her husband avoid blindness. She says her husband's outgoing, vivacious personality has changed "This could have been prevented, if we only knew," she says. NPR correspondent Sydney Lupkin contributed to this report. title: 16 cozy activities to add to your fall bucket list
summary: Carve a pumpkin? You can do better than that. Fun and unusual ways to celebrate the season, from writing a gratitude letter to making an ancestral altar.
content: By Malaka Gharib , Clare Marie Schneider , Marielle Segarra One clever way to celebrate the season? Put a rest day on your calendar. As the days shorten, you may feel lower energy when the sun sets at 5 p.m. instead of 8. So create the space in your life to recharge. Hannah Churn for NPR hide caption Never miss a story or episode from Life Kit. Sign up for our weekly newsletter to get our journalism delivered directly to your inbox. Many of us do the same things every year to celebrate the fall. We bust out the autumn wreath. Light the pumpkin spice candle. Pull those fuzzy sweaters out from the back of the closet. But there are so many other fun ways to make these coming months feel cozy. Here are 16 satisfying activities and rituals to add to your fall bucket list. As the days darken and plants prepare for winter dormancy, they embody the best of what the season has to offer: an opportunity for warmth, introspection and rest. Add this secret ingredient to your soup. Sohla El-Waylly, chef and author of Start Here: Instructions for Becoming A Better Cook , shares her secret superhero ingredient for making good soup : a pinch of MSG. It adds "a little bit of savory depth that makes you want to keep eating more." Switch from a cold breakfast to a hot one. It's tiny changes like this one that "reorient my attention from the negative things about the cold, dark and wet to the things I enjoy when the temperature drops," says Kari Leibowitz, a health psychologist and the author of How to Winter: Harness Your Mindset to Thrive on Cold, Dark, or Difficult Days . Cook this one-pan cheesy baked pasta dish. Food writer Melissa Clark loves cooking easy meals for her family with just one pan. This tactic, she says, can help reduce the time we spend cooking and cleaning — and leave us with more time for lounging. Try her recipe for this comforting baked pasta with tomato, sausage and ricotta . Write a gratitude letter. Got a quiet evening to spare? Think of someone in your life who you have not had the chance to thank, says psychologist Christina Costa. "Why are you grateful for that person? Think of a specific instance when they helped you. Then send them a letter, an email, or even better, deliver the letter in person and read it to them." If you're stuck, she says, "think of a K-12 teacher. That's going to give you a big boost." Expressed meaningfully, gratitude can have positive effects on our mental and physical health. Take stock of your holiday traditions. Before the holidays get into full swing, take a moment to reflect on your traditions so they feel more intentional, says clinical psychologist Andrea Bonior. What do you want a particular holiday or event to mean? "Is it about giving back to others? Gratitude? Finding the light in the darkness?" she says. If you're holding on to traditions out of obligation, or if they no longer feel meaningful, maybe it's time for a change. (This story has great advice on how to make new holiday traditions .) Decorate for all five senses. If you want your home to feel like a fall celebration, infuse the vibe more deeply throughout your home through sight, sound, scent, touch and taste , says interior designer Elaine Griffin. That might mean throwing a velvety blanket over the couch; getting a candle with a loud, crackling wick; hanging up a cinnamon broom; displaying decorative gourds; and keeping a tin of chocolate chip cookies in the kitchen. Rotate your cherished mementos. Make your home feel comforting and inspiring by swapping out the items you display in your house, says Sally Augustin, a psychologist who focuses on environment and design. Think of these items as a visiting exhibit that you can swap out every month . "It continually refreshes your familiar environment and gives you a feeling of control," she says. Replace a photo of you and your mom with a more recent one. Or swap the knick-knack you brought home from a vacation with a painting that a friend made you. Spend the morning reading in bed. Lynn Neary has been covering books for NPR for over a decade. In our episode on how to get into a reading habit , she told us: "I love to lie in bed and read — particularly on weekend mornings." It's a good way to start your day and you're less likely to fall asleep while reading, she adds. Refresh yourself before bed with an evening walk. Yes, even if it's dark and cold out. It makes you feel "awake but calm and ready for bed," says Leibowitz, who has studied how people survive in places with extreme winter. Don't let the weather discourage you. In Norway, she says, they have a saying: "There's no such thing as bad weather, only bad clothing." Create a home theater. Devika Girish , co-deputy editor of Film Comment Magazine , explains what you'll need to mimic the immersive experience of a movie theater at home. Watch the film on the biggest screen available to you (if you can, get a projector). Get some blankets. And fix yourself some snacks. Girish particularly loves munching on crisped chickpeas and popcorn and sipping a hot cup of cider while watching movies. Put a rest day on your calendar. As the days shorten, you may feel lower energy when the sun sets at 5 p.m. instead of 8. So create the space in your life to recharge. Tricia Hersey, author of the book Rest is Resistance: A Manifesto , likes to block off a rest day on her calendar each week. "I don't look at my email. I don't respond to anything work-related. I lay around the house." If you can't take a full rest day, take sensory breaks , says Dr. Saundra Dalton-Smith, author of Sacred Rest: Recover Your Life, Renew Your Energy, Restore Your Sanity . If you've been in virtual meetings all day, take five or 10 minutes to shut the screen and close your eyes. "It's similar to the reboot we do on our computers when it gets frozen and won't respond to us anymore. We do a hard reset, and everything's back to normal," she says. Alternatively, you can look out a window at a faraway object. That helps reduce eye strain. Let go of that feeling of FOMO. When you find yourself thinking the grass is greener on the other side, remind yourself why you're watering yours . "Maybe [you chose to stay in] because you had a long week and you need to recharge with some alone time. Or maybe you have an early start the next day. Whatever the reason might be, it's important to remember that as humans, we live by making a series of trade-offs," says clinical psychologist Aarti Gupta . Put one group activity you've been wanting to do on your calendar. If you are craving more community and connection this time of year, go ahead and make the first move. Try hosting something, anything. It doesn't even have to be at your home. "Start with something you feel sounds fun," says Priya Parker, author of The Art of Gathering . Invite three friends to visit a new bookshop across town. Go apple picking. Organize a horror movie-watching marathon. Create an ancestral altar. Create a place in your home to honor beloved family members and friends who have passed away. Display family heirlooms or tchotchkes that represent each ancestor. These things "carry an energetic signature that connects with our sense of history and our imagination, which will give us the parts of [our] history that may have been lost," says Camara Meri Rajabari , a psychotherapist who helps Black, Indigenous and people of color explore their ancestral roots. Make a powerful spiritual connection on your next nature walk. Lucretia VanDyke, author of African American Herbalism: A Practical Guide To Healing Plants And Folk Traditions , shares an exercise to help you create a profound connection to the flora and fauna around you. Think about how trees communicate with each other through their network of roots underground. Then interpret that connection as energy, VanDyke says. For example, if you are looking at a tree in Louisiana, and you miss your family in North Carolina, envision that network of trees and roots connecting you to them. You may start to imagine your "spirit being at home with them," she says. Email us at lifekit@npr.org with your response and full name, and we may feature your story on NPR. This digital story was edited by Meghan Keane. The visual editor is CJ Riculan. We'd love to hear from you. Email us at LifeKit@npr.org. title: A year of ceasefire in Gaza through the lens of NPR's reporter
summary: It has been one year since Hamas released the remaining Israeli hostages and President Trump promised an end to the war, but Palestinians say the past 12 months have been a ceasefire in name only.
content: By Anas Baba A Palestinian mother mourns her son, who was killed in an Israeli airstrike just over a month into the ceasefire, at Al-Shifa Hospital, in Gaza City, on Nov. 20, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption Editor's note: This story contains graphic images of violence and death. GAZA STRIP — President Donald Trump promised an end to Israel's war in Gaza after he pushed Israel to agree to a ceasefire and Hamas to release remaining Israeli hostages. The deal came into effect on Oct. 10, 2025. A year later, however, there's still no international peacekeeping force in Gaza as promised and no reconstruction. Instead, Israel's military has expanded its control to roughly 70% of Gaza, squeezing more than 2 million Palestinians near the sea's edge. Israel has also continued targeting Hamas throughout the ceasefire. Those attacks have killed more than 1,400 Palestinians this past year, nearly 500 of them women and children, according to Gaza's Health Ministry. Although the bombings have not stopped, they have slowed down during the ceasefire. That has given people in Gaza a chance to recover from what U.N.-backed experts declared was a famine in the north of the territory last year. More food is now entering, reversing starvation across Gaza. NPR's reporter in Gaza, Anas Baba, has been capturing moments of respite and continuous grief over the past 12 months of the ceasefire. Below are a selection of his photos. Palestinians returned to the ruins of Gaza City after Israeli forces withdrew and ended their ground operation on the first day of the ceasefire, on Oct. 10, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption In Khan Younis, families greet Palestinian prisoners who were freed in exchange for Israeli hostages on Oct. 13, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption At Al-Shifa Hospital on Oct. 23, 2025, Joud Al-Angar, 12, and his younger cousin are covered in dime-sized scabs after they were wounded by a piece of shrapnel from an Israeli munition. They found it in the rubble and thought it was coal they could use to help their family cook dinner. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption The bodies of multiple people, including children, are covered in shrouds at a morgue at Al-Shifa Hospital on Nov. 20, 2025, after Israeli airstrikes targeted homes and tents. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption People inspect the aftermath of a deadly Israeli airstrike that destroyed a home in Gaza City six weeks into the ceasefire on Nov. 20, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption A father and his son wade through flooded streets in Gaza City after picking up humanitarian aid on Nov. 25, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption Children wear virtual reality headsets as part of a TechMed Gaza initiative that aims to help provide children with psychosocial support for trauma, in Al-Zuweida, Gaza, on Dec. 10, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption Saqer Al-Ankah holds his dying 10-year-old granddaughter, Bayan, in his arms at Baptist Hospital in Gaza City on Dec. 10, 2025, after she was shot in her tent by Israeli troops who occupy northeast Gaza. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption Makeshift tents like these in Gaza City on Dec. 11, 2025, offer little protection from the winter cold, but the U.N. says roughly 1.5 million people have only these for shelter after Israeli airstrikes destroyed nearly all the buildings in the war. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption Raed el-Ghazawi and his children stand in a tent in Gaza City on Dec. 11, 2025. The family of five says the tent is freezing cold and damp from winter rainstorms. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption On Dec. 17, 2025, Palestinian Christian children decorate a Christmas tree inside the Holy Family Church in Gaza City for the first time since the beginning of the war. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption Fresh produce returns to Gaza City's streets on Dec. 23, 2025, after U.N.-backed experts declared a famine there amid Israeli restrictions on aid during the war. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption Patients sit in a clinic run by Doctors Without Borders in Gaza City on Dec. 31, 2025, a day before Israel banned more than 40 international aid organizations from bringing in staff or aid to Gaza. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption Palestinian female artists gather at the beach in Gaza City for the first time since the war began to paint as a form of therapy, on Feb. 12, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption Palestinian rescue workers begin the work of retrieving corpses from under the rubble of homes bombed by Israel during the war in Beit Lahia, Gaza, on Feb. 16, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption The skeleton of Shawqi Abu Naser, 60, is retrieved from under the rubble on Feb. 16, 2026, more than a year after an Israeli airstrike killed 132 people from the same family in Beit Lahia. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption A mother from the Abu Nasr family sits by her son's body in Beit Lahia on Feb. 17, 2026. The body was retrieved from under the rubble more than a year after 132 people were killed in a single Israeli airstrike on the family home. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption Palestinians gather in an open space in Gaza City for early morning prayers that mark the end of the Muslim holy month of Ramadan on March 20, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption A child smiles next to a man dressed as a clown on the first day of Eid al-Fitr, celebrations that mark the end of Ramadan fasting, in Gaza City on March 20, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption A Palestinian boy shakes hands with Hamas militants on the first day of Eid al-Fitr, following the end of the Muslim holy month of Ramadan, in Gaza City on March 20, 2026. Palestinians are barred from entering the area. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption A Palestinian child carries jugs of water as he passes by a mural of Spanish soccer star Lamine Yamal that is painted on the rubble of a home destroyed by Israeli airstrikes, in Al-Shati refugee camp, Gaza, on May 14, 2026. Aid organizations are restricted from entering the area. A teenage girl who was going to find internet access to take her final exams was killed in the strike. title: After losing ground with Latino voters, Democrats are turning to influencers for help
summary: Democrats are hoping to win back Latino voters who have soured on both parties. They hope Latino content creators will bridge the gap.
content: Claudia Grisales Democrats are trying to rebuild trust among Latino voters, and turning to content creators for help. Above, Spanish language voting stickers which read "He Votado Hoy" ("I Voted Today") at a Philadelphia polling place in 2019. Matt Rourke/AP hide caption Democrats lost the 2024 elections in part because of their eroding support among Latino voters, a constituency that was once a reliable segment of their base. That November, Kamala Harris won the Latino vote by three points, according to the Pew Research Center . In 2020, Joe Biden carried them by 25 points. This year, swing districts with large Hispanic populations could help decide which party controls the House. And Democrats are scrambling for ways to win those voters back. One new effort comes from the campaign arm of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, also known as BOLD PAC. In February, they launched a program to personally connect social media influencers with voters. "We're turning to trusted voices in local communities that have followings giving them information and then allowing them to create content in a way that is organic and authentic," said Rep. Linda Sánchez, D-Calif., who chairs BOLD PAC. That includes Latina content creator Alexa Flores, who not long ago mostly posted about beauty tips and fashion. But the Arizona resident shifted to politics in response to the Trump administration's immigration policies. She says she wants Latino voters to understand their impact if they vote. "My job is to get people to understand that so that they can go and move that needle," said Flores, who has nearly 500,000 followers across her platforms. Her job now includes "get-out-the-vote" events with BOLD PAC in swing districts around the country. Flores, for her part, will appear at a wine tasting event in Las Cruces, N.M. – where Democratic Rep. Gabe Vasquez is locked in a close race against Republican Greg Cunningham. She'll also appear at a Día de los Muertos event with lowriders and voters in Tucson, Ariz., where Marine veteran JoAnna Mendoza is trying to unseat GOP incumbent Juan Ciscomani. BOLD PAC says it is not paying content creators for posts. Instead, they're providing stipends of $1,500 for flights, hotels and other travel costs for each event. Sánchez says content creators could help bridge a gap for her party. Thirty percent of Latinos regularly get their news from influencers on social media, according to Pew Research Center . That's more than any other demographic. "So whether that's ... Instagram or YouTube or TikTok, that's how they're getting their information," she said. "So we need to be in those spaces." Rep. Linda Sánchez, D-Calif., chairs BOLD PAC. She says content creators can help bridge a gap for her party. Above, Sanchez speaks on immigration at the U.S. Capitol on May 10, 2023. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images hide caption Democratic strategist Stephanie Valencia says Democratic efforts to win back long term support from Latino voters is going to be an uphill battle. Valencia is co-founder of Equis Research, which estimates that roughly a third of Latinos are considered independent voters. Of those, more than 40% think neither party cares about people like them. "One election cycle is not going to solve the problem that Democrats have had and a frayed trust with Latino voters that has developed over the last several election cycles," Valencia said. In 2024, Latinos shifted right in response to what they saw as liberal immigration policies and a focus on foreign intervention over domestic policy under former President Biden. That year, President Trump grew his party's share of Latino votes by double digits to 48%, leaving Democrats with a slim majority, according to Pew Research Center . It's those kinds of swings that can cost a party a close election. This year, leaders at BOLD PAC sense an opportunity, as they've watched a growing number of Latinos say they feel betrayed by President Trump's immigration and economic policies. Still, Valencia warns that some Democratic campaigns continue to underestimate how "swingy" a good chunk of the Latino electorate is. That is, they show up with too little, too late when it comes to campaign spending and messaging. "Latinos are just a more persuadable universe and can't just be treated as a base turnout universe for Democrats," she said. Solangie Hernandez Hollowell, a Texas influencer who is also working with BOLD PAC, agrees. Like others, her posts often don't even mention specific candidates, but they do focus on issues that Democrats are campaigning on this cycle – issues like taxes and immigration. So she wants to help Latinos connect with candidates in a way that goes beyond the transactional. "Latinos feel like politicians show up just right before the election. I don't feel like we feel very heard," she said. So she's translating what this political moment can mean for them. "My main goal right now is making sure that everything that's happening around the world reaches my family and my community in a way that they can understand it," she said. Flores, the Arizona influencer, says she hopes for more awareness that Latinos are having a growing impact on major pieces of American life. "The wave of Latinos growing in this country is becoming a bigger voice for a lot of things," she said. NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. title: The Met puts a modern artist front and center (and there's some Jackson Pollock, too)
summary: In a blockbuster show, The Metropolitan Museum of Art places the work of two major 20th century artists side by side: the married couple Lee Krasner and Jackson Pollock.
content: Anastasia Tsioulcas When Lee Krasner was asked in a 1978 interview what she was doing while her husband Jackson Pollock was becoming so famous, she said, "I was working all the time." Krasner is shown above, at work, in 1981. Ernst Haas/Getty Images hide caption There's a new blockbuster show at New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art. Past Continuous features two artists: Jackson Pollock, with many of his instantly recognizable "drip" paintings, and Lee Krasner, an artist often overshadowed by Pollock, who was her husband. But in this major exhibition, Krasner is finally getting her due — and on her own terms. This gargantuan show is replete with Pollock's greatest hits, the giant, frozen dances of paint splashed on canvas that have become iconic. But this exhibition of more than 120 works (74 from Krasner, and 48 from Pollock) reveals Krasner as an Abstract Expressionist titan, too. One of the first works that catches your eye is a 1955 Krasner collage. "Collage was very catalytic for her at these crucial moments in her life," said Brinda Kumar, one of the two Met curators who put together this exhibition. "She was literally sometimes tearing up older bodies of work to create a new chapter." This work is 1955's Bald Eagle , a riotous mix of browns, blacks, fuchsia, and orange, with a claw-like slash of yellow. And right in the middle is a cutout whose shape evokes the head of a bald eagle — and that's the name that Krasner gave to this collage. Lee Krasner, Bald Eagle, 1955, Oil, paper, and canvas collage on linen,  ASOM Collection 2026 Pollock-Krasner Foundation/Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York hide caption Pollock's rejects were the source material for Bald Eagle , according to Kumar. "Krasner has very intentionally and deliberately cut up discarded Pollock works from this era in the 1950s, where you can see his distinctive drip still evident," she said. When you put Krasner's collages next to Pollock's drip paintings, we see something new in the juxtaposition, said another Met curator, David Breslin. "But that doesn't mean that the individual parts forgo their histories or their pasts," Breslin said. "We see that almost as a metaphor for couples in relationships as well. You form a unit, yet you also have all the things in your head, in your mind, in your heart that are your own, that don't change." And sure enough, just past these collages, a visitor will see one of Pollock's classic drip paintings — 1952's Convergence , with neon orange and electric yellow so bright and bold that they foreshadow 1980s subway graffiti. The curators have put Convergence on a freestanding wall near windows, with daylight shining through — evoking the energy of a contemporary gallery. Installation view of Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous, on view at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Oct. 4, 2026 – Jan. 31, 2027. Anna-Marie Kellen/The Met hide caption The unspoken challenge of this show is to invite comparisons between wife-and-husband artists. In popular imagination, Pollock is often the troubled genius and hero, and Krasner is sidelined as a helpmate. She knew what people thought — but she didn't care. In a 1978 interview on a television program called Inside New York's Art World , the interviewer asked Krasner what she was doing while Pollock was becoming so famous. "I was working all the time," Krasner replied. "I doubt our relationship could have existed at all if I weren't working. In terms of what other people think, I can't do anything about that. You know, that's not my preoccupation anyway. As long as I was able to work, I went about my business." That's true, but Krasner was also very savvy about her market value as a female artist, said curator Brinda Kumar. Lee Krasner, Mosaic Table, 1947 Mosaic of mixed media (including broken glass, keys, coins, ceramic, and pebbles) in cement; iron wagon-wheel armature with steel Anna-Marie Kellen/The Met hide caption "She was very cognizant of the gender dynamics and the gender politics. His career was the one that was more successful at the time." To that end, she made certain calculations. They made their home in Springs, N.Y., a small fishing community on the far side of Long Island — a location Krasner chose specifically to get Pollock away from the business and booze of Manhattan. Pollock used a barn on the property to work on his enormous canvases, while Krasner painted first in the kitchen and then in a small, upstairs bedroom. Lee Krasner was all about reinvention — both artistic and personal. Born Lena Krassner in Brooklyn, she was the child of Orthodox Jewish parents who came from a shtetl in what is now Ukraine. Nobody in her family knew anything about art. She gave herself a series of new names: first Lenore, then Lee Krasner. She sculpted a new life as a young, bold artist. And she became a quintessential networker who knew everybody in New York's art scene. Journalist Mary Gabriel has written extensively about Krasner, including in her 2018 book Ninth Street Women: Lee Krasner, Elaine de Kooning, Grace Hartigan, Joan Mitchell, and Helen Frankenthaler: Five Painters and the Movement that Changed Modern Art . Gabriel says that unlike her husband, Krasner kept reinventing her style. "Krasner was so fascinating because she changed, not even by the decade. Every few years, she tries something new," Gabriel said. "She was always searching, which in a way is the most, I think, honest way to be an artist, because art is about discovery." These include what Krasner called her "Little Images" — densely populated paintings from the late 1940s of nearly hieroglyphic looking symbols, all jostling for space on small canvases — as well as immense works she created, especially after Pollock died in a car crash in 1956. Pollock was plagued by alcoholism and depression, and he cheated on her; his girlfriend of the time was one of the passengers in the crash. Krasner continued to be financially savvy as well. After Pollock's death, she more than tripled the price of one of his most famous works, Autumn Rhythm (Number 30) , to sell it to the Met — a sum that not just set the pace for Pollock's market value, but for a tide of modern artists. For this show, Autumn Rhythm was moved off its traditional museum wall to a freestanding display, Kumar noted. "It is almost architectural in a way, because it's set against this slate grey color," she said. "The swirling blacks get animated in a whole new way, and the familiar teals and the familiar whites surge with a new energy." Krasner seized upon her own new energy in the years after Pollock's death. She took over the barn studio that had been her husband's — and made giant, joyful work, brimming with life and lushness, as curator David Breslin noted. Lee Krasner, The Seasons, 1957, Oil and house paint on canvas, Whitney Museum of American Art The Pollock-Krasner Foundation/Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York hide caption "You see this incredible painting that's almost 17 feet wide called The Seasons , that has these forms and bodies, eyes and body parts and these things that look like vegetation sprawling out of it," Breslin said. "So she makes, almost in a contradictory way, some of the brightest, most vibrant paintings the year after his death." And in some way, this whole show is all about Lee Krasner finally being able to claim her own space. Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous runs at the Met until Jan. 31. title: Controversial vaccine trial touted by RFK Jr gets go-ahead in Guinea-Bissau
summary: Recommended dose of hepatitis B vaccine will be withheld from thousands of newborns by Danish researchers A controversial research trial that will withhold hepatitis B vaccines from some African newborns was given approval to move forward this week. It is a central part of the vaccine vision for Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime vaccine opponent. Continue reading...
content: Recommended dose of hepatitis B vaccine will be withheld from thousands of newborns by Danish researchers A controversial research trial that will withhold hepatitis B vaccines from some African newborns was given approval to move forward this week. It is a central part of the vaccine vision for Robert F Kennedy Jr , the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime vaccine opponent. At an anti-vaccine conference last month, Kennedy praised the Danish researchers behind the trial and touted US-supported research on hepatitis B in newborns as exemplifying the Trump administration’s agenda for vaccines, which has included slashing vaccine recommendations and casting doubt on the safety and effectiveness of shots. Kennedy “wants to make it so we don’t use a birth dose here in this country,” said Paul Offit, an infectious disease physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “That’s the goal.” Kennedy would never be able to do the trial in the US because of its significant ethical concerns, Offit added. “He’s taking advantage of a developing country … Is it because children in Africa are more expendable than children here?” Danish researchers plan to enroll 14,000 infants in Guinea-Bissau in the trial, giving the hepatitis B vaccine to half of the babies at birth and withholding it from the others for the first six weeks of life. An ethics committee at the researchers’ home institution of the University of Southern Denmark voted this week to proceed with the trial, and officials in Guinea-Bissau have also greenlit the project, which the health minister, Quinhin Nantote, initially said was suspended after international uproar earlier this year. Stig Børsen Hansen, a founding member who was one of two reviewers who presented the study to the Danish committee, resigned from the group in protest on Friday, citing major ethical issues with the study. “You are now enrolling newborns in a lottery to test a hypothesis,” Hansen said. The children who are randomly selected not to receive the birth dose of the vaccine, those who “lost the lottery”, face in their earliest days the risk of contracting hepatitis B, which can cause irreversible lifelong damage. “They contract hepatitis B in the context of being part of a research project,” Hansen said, which made their infection happen, in effect, “by design”. Three other members of the committee have also resigned in protest. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has reportedly set aside $1.6m in this year’s budget for the project, and it will be matched with private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation, which was co-founded by the billionaire activist Bill Ackman, and the Bluebell Foundation. The CDC, the Danish researchers, Pershing Square and Nantote have not responded to the Guardian’s questions about this trial. The news that the trial was approved by the Denmark ethics committee was first reported on Thursday by CIDRAP News . This is the first time details of the updated protocol have been disclosed. The Guinea-Bissau study protocol has changed since it was posted in January, according to details shared with the Guardian. The researchers will now test mothers for hepatitis B before they give birth. The babies of mothers who test positive will be given the vaccine and will not be included in the trial. But the babies of mothers whose tests are negative may be enrolled. The new protocol has not been shared publicly. In previous research, half of children who contracted hepatitis B did so after birth, through community exposures. “This virus can be transmitted casually,” Offit said. It can live on surfaces for up to seven days, and it can be acquired by sharing washcloths, toothbrushes and fingernail clippers. In addition, the hepatitis B test has a 5% false negative rate, which could provide false assurance that a birthing parent does not have the virus. Decades of research make it clear that the vaccine would be beneficial, which means it would be unfair to place some children in the vaccinated group and some children in the unvaccinated group, said Henrik Støvring, a professor of statistics and pharmacometrics at Aarhus University in Denmark . According to the Helsinki declaration, international medical research must be approved by ethics committees in both the host and sponsor countries. The Danish research ethics committee at the University of Southern Denmark had never considered medical studies before, but it changed the rules in order to vote on this one. While committee members with expertise argued against approving it, the majority ruled to move forward. “It’s very unusual to bring this into a committee like that,” Støvring said. The national ethics committee in Denmark oversees medical research, but this study was outside of their purview because it won’t take place in Denmark. Yet “I don’t see why you couldn’t do it in Denmark,” Støvring said of the trial. In fact, several conditions make it a better location. The hepatitis B vaccine is not usually given to newborns in Denmark unless the mother is positive for the virus, for which all pregnant people are tested in Denmark. Guinea-Bissau has some of the highest rates of hepatitis B in the world, with about 18% of adults carrying the virus. While it may be transmitted from mother to child during birth, it could also be transmitted from another parent, relatives, siblings or caregivers. Children who are infected with hepatitis B in the first year of life are significantly more likely to develop severe outcomes, including chronic infection and liver cancer. The Bandim Health Project, run by Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, has operated in Guinea-Bissau for decades and is closely enmeshed in the country’s health system. At least one top official, the current director of public health, held a dual appointment with Bandim as recently as December. Kennedy praised the Danish researchers at a recent anti-vaccine conference, calling them “the deities of vaccine research”. Kennedy claimed that a prior study they conducted indicated that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight.” He did not mention that another follow-up study from the same researchers found no effects at all. This study will focus on vaccination and mortality, as well as outcomes such as skin conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. “The main problem of this trial is that you have some very well-known bad diseases that you can protect with this vaccine,” Støvring said. “And what they then want to study is something highly speculative – in a situation where WHO and others are saying that you should give this vaccine at birth, period.” When asked about the study in a Thursday briefing, an official with the Africa CDC, which has opposed the trial, said there were “ongoing discussions” between the US and Guinea-Bissau and more details would be shared shortly. Guinea-Bissau planned to begin vaccinating all newborns against hepatitis B in 2027, but they pushed the campaign back to 2028. Kennedy and the Danish researchers were “taking advantage of that delay in practicing standard care to put these children at risk unnecessarily”, Offit said. “What a terrible thing to do. What a horribly unethical and cruel thing to do.”

title: ICJ judge Navi Pillay wins Nobel peace prize for promoting international law
summary: Committee recognises work of South African who chaired UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza . content: Committee recognises work of South African who chaired UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza  The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza . The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”. “Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” the committee said, mentioning her early work defending Nelson Mandela under South Africa’s apartheid regime, serving on the international criminal tribunal, and then as the UN high commissioner for human rights, as well as chairing the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory. That commission concluded last year that the state of Israel was guilty of genocidal acts in Gaza “with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza”, and said the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, its president, Isaac Herzog, and its former defence minister Yoav Gallant had “incited the commission of genocide”. “It is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the genocide convention,” Pillay said on the publication of the commission’s findings in September last year. Israel refused to cooperate with the commission, arguing it was biased, and rejected its report as “scandalous”. The Israeli foreign ministry reacted furiously to news of Pillay’s award on Friday. “If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner,” the ministry said on X , adding: “Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice. “Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.” In its statement , the Nobel committee said Pillay, 85, had “contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law”. “Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time,” the committee said. “In awarding this year’s Nobel peace prize , the Norwegian Nobel committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently,” its statement said. The committee said it had not been able to locate Pillay before its announcement on Friday morning. She was attending a meeting of human rights lawyers and jurists in Nuremberg, Germany, at the site of postwar war crimes trials of Nazi leaders, and heard the news from colleagues. She responded with disbelief. “I don’t know about it so much. The question is: is it true? Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify it,” she said. “The last thing I did was the report on Gaza naming what’s happening there as genocide,” Pillay added. “One of the main reactions to that report was people [complimented] me for my courage. You can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth. You interpret the law. You look at all the facts, so it’s an impartial decision.” Pillay is currently overseeing a genocide case against Myanmar at the ICJ. The ICJ, a UN body, rules on disputes between states, while the international criminal court (ICC) investigates and prosecutes individuals accused of atrocities and other grave international crimes. Hours after the announcement, the Trump administration unveiled broad new sanctions against the ICC, on which Pillay also once served. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the measures were to ensure the court would never prosecute Americans. The ICC has not charged any US nationals, and has previously pointed out that it is a court of last resort, unnecessary in the case of countries with effective legal systems. Last year, Donald Trump, who has long coveted the Nobel peace prize, imposed personal sanctions against ICC officials deemed to be involved in investigations of Americans or Israelis. The new sanctions target the court as an institution, blocking any ICC assets in the US and giving US companies and individuals six months to wind down any business with the court. The ICC said the sanctions were “an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the court from doing what it was created to do”. “It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law,” the court said in a statement. Pillay’s award was welcomed by human rights activists and hailed in South Africa , home to four previous laureates. The country’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, said: “Justice Pillay’s crowning as winner of the Nobel prize allows us to celebrate the progressive contributions she has made to strengthen peace, uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally.” Edwin Cameron, a retired South African constitutional court justice, said: “The award of the prize to Navi Pillay re-emphasises that the prize embodies an international aspiration to peace, and to respect and understanding across borders – and that leaders of great stature in our country – [Desmond] Tutu, Mandela, now Pillay – are recognised outside it, on the international stage. “This may help reset our national debate on South Africa’s position in the region, and in Africa,” he said. Yasmin Sooka, a human rights lawyer and commissioner on both South Africa and Sierra Leone’s truth and reconciliation commissions, said Pillay “follows in the footsteps of Chief Albert Luthuli and Archbishop Desmond Tutu, carrying forward South Africa’s proud tradition of linking peace with justice and human dignity”. “From defending apartheid’s most vulnerable to her pioneering role in the Akayesu judgment , she has transformed international justice. That judgment helped establish rape and sexual violence as weapons of war – a historic breakthrough that placed survivors’ experiences at the heart of international justice,” Sooka said. In 1998, the international criminal tribunal for Rwanda found Jean-Paul Akayesu, a former mayor of Taba, guilty of genocide and crimes against humanity. “At the ICC, as UN high commissioner for human rights, and leading the inquiry that found Israel responsible for genocide in Gaza, she has brought unwavering integrity and courage to holding power accountable,” Sooka added. Last year’s award of the peace prize to the Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, drew widespread criticism because of her calls for US military intervention in her country. Machado heightened the controversy in January by handing her winner’s medal to Trump. The prize committee insisted that the honour of being a Nobel laureate could not be transferred. On Friday, Pillay joked that she could do the same: “If you clap a little bit more, I’m going to share this prize with Trump.”

title: Isaias strengthens to become first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 season
summary: Storm expected to make landfall on US’s northern Gulf coast with risk of flash floods and isolated river flooding Isaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, with wind speeds of 80mph and a minimum pressure of 975mb. content: Storm expected to make landfall on US’s northern Gulf coast with risk of flash floods and isolated river flooding Isaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, with wind speeds of 80mph and a minimum pressure of 975mb. It is expected to strengthen to a category 2 hurricane as it approaches the US’s northern Gulf coast on Friday, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). As a result of the strong El Niño , it has been a notably quiet Atlantic hurricane season. The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which pre-dates the satellite era (1960s) for tracking hurricanes that has allowed for more non-landfall hurricanes to be discovered. Isaias is expected to make landfall on Friday evening local time, bringing an estimated 75-150mm (2.9-5.9in) of rainfall across the Gulf coast. There may be up to 250mm in places, with a possibility of flash flooding and isolated river flooding. The NOAA also said there was increasing likelihood of life-threatening storm surge along portions of the northern Gulf coast and damaging hurricane-force winds over portions of the Florida panhandle, southern Alabama and Mississippi . A hurricane warning has been issued and people have been told to prepare for long power outages and to obey any evacuation orders issued. In Zimbabwe , a state of disaster was declared in the south-east Masvingo province on Tuesday after a severe hailstorm caused widespread damage to homes and critical infrastructure. Preliminary assessments found the roofs had been torn off 8,500 homes. A further 15,300 people reported shattered windows, leaving many exposed to the elements as the rainy season begins. The country’s power infrastructure was badly affected, disrupting drainage and sewerage systems, raising concerns about public health. In Australia, a rare tornado hit the town of Ulladulla, about 140 miles (230km) south of Sydney, on 3 October. Tornadoes are relatively rare in Australia, where there are about 50 each year. This Ulladulla tornado damaged properties and felled trees.

title: Egyptian journalists plan weekend protest over detention of six colleagues
